reviews.text: The new-build subdivision as site of erasure — topsoil trucked in to bury what was there before, the cul-de-sac curving 'like a closing hand.' This story understands that domesticity is always built on displaced ground, that the amended soil is never just soil. The structural withholding is precise: we never learn what happened, but the empty fourth bedroom, Ellen Pavlick's pregnancy, the lavender torn out at dawn — the negative space tells us everything. I am less convinced by the fox as symbol. It works early, when the vixen is simply present and watching, but the dream sequence where it fills a room 'the way a body fills a bath' pushes toward allegory where implication was already sufficient. Still, the line about their silence being 'load-bearing' is one of the best sentences I have read about marriage this year.

Good atmosphere, properly unsettling in places. The bit where Gil crawls under the house and comes back with that blank expression — that's genuine dread, that is. But I kept waiting for the story to arrive somewhere and it never quite does. The fox, the room, the soil — it's all hovering. Some readers like that. I wanted one more turn of the screw.

This wrecked me quietly. The scene where Ellen comes over with brownies and Nora looks at her belly and feels 'something pressing at the base of her throat like a thing swallowed wrong' — I had to put my phone down. The story never names the loss but it saturates every detail, the too-eager garden, the room nobody enters, Gil's compulsive repairs. Grief as architecture. And that ending, where the iced tea 'tasted like their life — clean, slightly sweet, made with care by a man who loved her in the way he knew how,' just devastated me. The fox watching from the fence is Nora's own wildness, the part of her that refuses the suburban containment, and I love that the story doesn't resolve whether that wildness is salvation or threat.

Okay I'm bringing this to book club immediately. It's short enough to read in one sitting and then you could argue about what happened for an hour. The fourth bedroom! Nobody ever says what it was for! And the garden growing too fast, and Gil under the house for forty minutes — this is suburban horror done right. My favorite detail is the twin bicycles lying on their sides with wheels pointing at the sky. That image is going to stay with me.

A controlled exercise in domestic gothic that works through accumulation rather than event. The prose has a recursive quality — sentences that circle back and extend themselves, mirroring Nora's avoidance — that recalls the better European traditions of interior horror. The central metaphor (amended soil covering what was there before) earns its weight because the story applies it structurally, not just imagistically: the entire narrative is amended, covering what was there before. Particularly effective is the way Gil's competence becomes monstrous — not through malice but through its relentless, caulk-gun adequacy. The ending refuses closure without feeling incomplete, which is harder than it looks.

This one does real damage. The genius is in what's withheld — that fourth bedroom operates like a wound the house has grown around. Nora routing past it, feeling the coolness on her face, never turning the handle. And Gil's response to every problem being another repair, another exclusion door, another sealed breach. 'The conversation they were not having was not, precisely, a conversation that either of them had refused' — that's not gothic decoration, that's a marriage caught in amber. The fox sequence in the backyard, where its open mouth is described as 'not a threat' but 'a fact,' genuinely chilled me.

Pretty writing. Really pretty writing. But is it scary? The fox watches, the garden grows, the room stays closed, Gil caulks things. I kept wanting the story to bite and it just... breathes at you. The crawl space scene had real tension and then it deflated into another paragraph of Nora feeling things she can't name. I get what it's doing — the horror is the not-saying — but at some point you have to say something or you're just withholding for style points.

Well-crafted atmosphere and I liked how every detail — the soil, the roses, the foxes — connects to the central mystery. But the ending left me unsatisfied. She touches the door, doesn't open it, goes downstairs for iced tea. I understand ambiguity in horror but this felt like the story stopped rather than ended. Gil crawling under the house was the strongest scene. The 'something breathing' under the exclusion door in the last line was effective but I wanted more from the buildup.
